title: Pollice Verso
source: Phoenix Art Museum, Phoenix, Arizona (museum purchase, 1968; public domain). Wikimedia Commons: Jean-Leon Gerome Pollice Verso.jpg (2425 x 1630 px)
caption: One gesture, one painting, and an idea about Rome that everyone still believes. #gladiator #ancientrome #gerome #arthistory #didyouknow
_verify: VERIFIED, Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollice_Verso_(Gérôme)): 1872, oil on canvas, 96.5 x 149.2 cm, Phoenix Art Museum; spectators give the thumbs-down to the victorious gladiator; the defeated retiarius raises two fingers pleading for mercy; the Vestal Virgins among the spectators signal death; the emperor watches from his box; the exact gesture behind 'pollice verso' is unknown (up, down, horizontal or hidden in the fist); the painting did much to popularise thumbs up = life, thumbs down = death.

VERIFIED, Phoenix Art Museum blog (phxart.org/?p=29472): 'pollice verso simply means with a turned thumb'; no historical record confirms thumbs-down meant death; begun before 1869, finished 1872 after a pause for the Franco-Prussian War; acquired by PhxArt in 1968; the victor looks up to the crowd 'or perhaps the Roman emperor himself' for permission.

VERIFIED, Gladiator: Wikipedia EN and Artnet (news.artnet.com/art-world/gladiator-painting-film-2581507): producers Walter Parkes and Douglas Wick showed Ridley Scott a reproduction of the painting before he read the script; Scott: 'That image spoke to me of the Roman Empire in all its glory and wickedness.' Slide 9 paraphrases, no quote on the slide.

VERIFIED, Vestals: Eclectic Light (eclecticlight.co/2018/07/26/too-real-the-narrative-paintings-of-jean-leon-gerome-4/) counts a row of six Vestals at the right, described by critics as 'baying for blood'; Encyclopaedia Romana (penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/gladiators/polliceverso.html): Prudentius describes a Vestal turning her thumb to urge the kill; Suetonius says Vestals had their own seats at the games.

VERIFIED with nuance, the emperor's final word: Artnet says the gesture was typically reserved for the emperor when present; Encyclopaedia Romana cites Anthony Corbeill that the editor of the games conveyed the verdict. Slide 6 only says the emperor watches and the decision is his, which fits the painting's scene.

UNVERIFIED, not used: the emperor eating (figs or other food) in his box. No source I could read (Wikipedia, PhxArt, Artnet, GetDailyArt, LACMA, Eclectic Light) mentions it; Rampley & Co. describes him 'watching over the victor with glee'. Check on the full image before mentioning it in a comment.

VERIFIED, not on slides: winner identified as a murmillo (Wikipedia) or secutor (GetDailyArt); armour based on finds from Pompeii, with inaccuracies. Slides say only 'bronze helmet'. A.T. Stewart bought it for 80,000 francs (Wikipedia).
Focus boxes estimated from the contact sheet thumbnail; re-tune on the real image. Kept away from the bodies and the blood on the sand (slide 4 frames only the raised hand).

slides.headline: You know this gesture. Rome might not.
Inside the Colosseum
slides.text: 1872. Gérôme takes us into the Colosseum. The fight is over, the winner stands over his opponent, and the whole arena waits for one signal.

slides.headline: The victor waits
slides.text: The winner, face hidden behind a gleaming bronze helmet, looks up at the stands. He will not strike until Rome decides.

slides.headline: Two fingers raised
slides.text: Beneath him, the beaten fighter lifts two fingers, begging for mercy. But up in the front row, the answer is already coming.

slides.headline: The Vestal Virgins
slides.text: Look closer: Rome's holiest priestesses, sworn to purity, lean over the wall and demand his death, thumbs turned firmly down.

slides.headline: The emperor watches
slides.text: Meanwhile, in his shaded box, the emperor watches. The crowd has made its wish clear. Now the decision is his.

slides.headline: Pollice verso
slides.text: But here's the twist: 'pollice verso' simply means 'with a turned thumb'. No Roman text tells us which way it turned.

slides.headline: A painter's guess
slides.text: Up, down, sideways, hidden in the fist: historians still argue. Gérôme's picture is what made 'thumbs down means death' stick.

slides.headline: From canvas to Gladiator
slides.text: Over a century later, producers showed Ridley Scott this image and he signed on to direct Gladiator. What do you think Romans really did?
